//: L-loc7: the delta's wildlife.  dda's spawn groups are North American; the species below that have a close Vietnamese relative living the same way are redescribed in place (same id, so their eggs, young and corpses still work), the rest leave the spawn groups (wildlife_groups.json).  Sprites are dda's.
description: A quạ, glossy black from beak to tail, with a heavy arched bill.  Crows follow the rice harvest and the rubbish heaps; this one watches you with interest, as if you might drop something.
A chim sẻ, the small brown sparrow with a chestnut cap and a black spot on each white cheek that nests under every roof tile in the south.
A sáo, a dark brown starling with a black head, a yellow bill and a bare yellow patch behind each eye.  Bold, loud and clever, it walks rather than hops.
A cốc đế, a small black diving bird that fishes the rivers and canals, then stands on a stake with its wings spread out to dry.
A gà nước, a dark water bird with a red shield above its yellow-tipped bill.  It picks its way across water hyacinth on long green toes.
A le hôi, a small round diving bird of ponds and flooded fields.  It vanishes underwater at the first sign of trouble and comes up somewhere else.
A rái cá, a sleek brown otter of the mangrove creeks and canals, hunting fish in family groups.  The Cần Giờ forest is its home; the empty fish ponds are its larder now.
A heo rừng, bristly, dark and short-tempered.  Wild pigs still root in the forest of Củ Chi and the mangroves of Cần Giờ, and farm pigs gone loose have joined them.
A striped heo rừng piglet.  Where there is one, its mother is not far away.
A rắn nước, an olive water snake with a black chequer pattern.  It hunts frogs and fish in the rice fields and is quick to bite but harmless.
A young rắn nước, no longer than a pencil.
A rùa ba gờ, a small dark turtle with three ridges along its shell and pale stripes on its face, at home in ponds, canals and paddies.
A rùa ba gờ hatchling, the size of a coin.
An ếch Mỹ.  American bullfrogs have been farmed in the delta since the 1990s, and the ones that got out of their pens now boom in every canal.
An ếch đồng, the fat brown-green frog of the paddies that every child in the delta has caught for dinner.
A rice-field frog that has suffered some kind of mutation.  At its hips it has clusters of extra legs, some complete, others ending at the first joint.
A cóc nhà, the warty brown toad that comes out on wet nights to eat insects under the street lamps.  The glands behind its eyes ooze a poison that has killed people who ate it.
A cá lóc, a long, mottled, toothy fish that breathes air and can live in a puddle of mud through the dry season.  Grilled in straw, it is a delta classic.
A cá rô phi, a deep-bodied grey fish farmed in every pond in the south.  It has escaped into the canals as well.
A cá tra, a big pale catfish of the Mekong and its rafts of fish cages.  Exported by the shipload as 'basa'.
A cá trê, a slippery catfish that breathes air and wriggles across wet ground from one pond to the next.
A cá rô đồng, a small spiny fish of the paddies, famous for crawling out of the water after rain.
A lươn, a smooth yellow-brown eel that burrows in the mud of rice fields and canals.
A cá chép, the golden-bronze carp of ponds and temples.  On the 23rd of the twelfth month every family releases one to carry the Kitchen Gods to heaven.

//: Only Thảo Cầm Viên has bears (and deer and tigers) now; the zoo's animals do not breed into the wild.
description: A gấu ngựa, a black bear with a white crescent on its chest and big round ears.  The zoo took in bears rescued from the bile farms; this one has nothing left to lose.
A young gấu ngựa, its chest crescent still faint.  Its mother is somewhere close.
A nai, a big shaggy brown deer with a dark mane and rough antlers, from the zoo's deer park.  It startles at every sound.
A young nai, still unsteady on its legs.
A mèo Xiêm, cream with dark ears, face, paws and tail, and loud about everything.  The breed came from next door.
This ferocious cow-sized mantis stalks the rice fields.  It is probably capable of killing a buffalo with its powerful arms.
A rắn hổ mang, brown with a pale ring on the back of its hood.  It rears up and spreads that hood when you come close; its bite can kill a man in an hour.
A young rắn hổ mang.  It is already venomous.
A chuột đồng, a sleek brown rat of the paddies and dykes.  It eats the harvest, and in the delta the harvest eats it back: grilled with lemongrass, it was a market dish.
A cu gáy, a soft brown dove with a black collar dotted white.  Its slow 'cu cu gáy' call is the sound of a delta morning.
A cò trắng, a slender white heron with black legs and yellow feet, wading the paddies for fish and frogs.  The folk songs are full of it.
A nutritious egg laid by a myna.  The shell is a glossy pale blue.
